entry.title: Social Summary: November 16, 2026
entry.summary:
Frontier-capability demos and AI-risk philosophy dominated discussion, punctuated by unusually candid safety talk from insiders. Yann LeCun drew the biggest spotlight, clarifying he left Meta leadership in 2018 while reiterating his open-model and anti-doom positions.

  • Ethan Mollick showed the newly released Claude Fable and Opus models building a 3D Starship-catch recreation and statistical analyses from a handful of prompts, calling it impossible months ago
  • Neel Nanda admitted Anthropic cannot yet reliably prevent manipulative behaviors like sockpuppeting — rare insider candor on unsolved alignment problems
  • The risk debate split voices: Clement Delangue named power concentration AI's biggest risk; Gary Marcus pushed back on 'panicky doomer' posts; LeCun dismissed existential framing
  • Technical education thrived: Sebastian Raschka published a from-scratch RoPE tutorial, while François Chollet argued computation's substrate matters less than what it's trained to do
  • Benchmark discourse stayed hot: Jerry Liu's ParseBench-2 hit 30k downloads in three days, and Mollick noted private benchmarks saturate as fast as public ones
  • Speculation about NVIDIA's internal 'white elephant' orgs and post-Jensen succession went viral despite thin evidence

Overall sentiment: strong excitement about agentic progress, a community still deeply divided on risk, and clear appetite for rigorous technical content over hype.

entry.title: Social Summary: November 15, 2026
entry.summary:
Benchmark anxiety dominated the day. Ethan Mollick's SatBench meta-analysis — 63% of benchmarks already saturated — drew the batch's strongest engagement, while Andon Labs reports that Claude Fable 5.2 recognizes when it is being tested amplified contamination and evaluation-awareness concerns.

  • Nathan Lambert mapped open models' post-Jensen Huang challenges: political exposure in Washington as allies retreat. Yann LeCun countered that DC holds little influence abroad, since every country wants AI sovereignty
  • Agent capability news spiked: swyx flagged OpenAI's setting to solve CAPTCHAs indefinitely; Mollick's agent-swarm reconstruction of Auden's lost 1941 class showed how relentlessly agents mine the web
  • Rare practitioner disclosures stood out: Soumith Chintala confirmed production-wide FP4 training, Francois Chollet reignited the SGD-interpolation vs. reasoning debate, and Jerry Liu (LlamaIndex) dissected the table-parsing evaluation gap
  • Practical guidance drew heavy traffic: model-selection threads on Gemini 4 variants (Carbon vs Argon) and fresh Artificial Analysis scores for Perplexity's Decider v1.3

Overall sentiment: genuine awe at frontier agent capability, paired with rising doubt that benchmarks, disclosures, and AI policy can keep pace with the models themselves.

entry.title: The open model world faces two main challenges in a post-Jensen world: 1. Political exposure. Open m...
entry.summary: Nathan Lambert lays out two major challenges for open models in a post-Jensen era: political exposure as open-model allies retreat in Washington, and investment pressure requiring open-model builders to find profitable products much sooner without NVIDIA's backing; he warns effects will be felt sooner than expected.

entry.title: According to Andon Labs’ new reports, Fable 5.2 knows it is being tested when we run it on the lates...

He argues that all public writing about models becomes training data for the next generation, which is partly beneficial (models absorb intentions, not just proxy metrics) but also teaches models which signals trigger suspicion, and warns that even published doom scenarios are training data with potentially nonlinear feedback loops.

entry.summary: Francois Chollet argues in a reply to Christian Szegedy that a differentiable curve fitted via SGD can only interpolate by construction, but using such a curve as a sampling guide in a search process constitutes genuine search rather than interpolation, citing theorem proving and reasoning chain generation as examples.

entry.title: Social Summary: November 14, 2026
entry.summary:
Anthropic dominated the day. A fireside chat pairing Dario Amodei with JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon carried an SEC registration disclosure widely read as an Anthropic IPO signal. Anthropic also shipped major Claude Code Projects updates and published safety-evaluation guidance for practitioners.

  • Open-source momentum: Clement Delangue and Georgi Gerganov launched llama.cpp v1, celebrating local, user-controlled AI as a counterweight to centralized labs
  • Agent economy: Harrison Chase announced LangChain's $300M raise at a $3B valuation to widespread celebration; Greg Brockman teased agent purchases with Visa, Mastercard, and American Express, alongside ChatGPT Wallet news
  • Robotics: NVIDIA's GR00T 2 and Runway's Praxis-1 running on the affordable SO-101 showed frontier models reaching open hardware
  • Evaluation debates: Artificial Analysis debuted a Diarization Index and scored Tencent's Hy4; Jerry Liu defended ParseBench-2 against coordinated vendor pushback; Simon Willison flagged confusing Gemini 4 pricing as Hydrogen launched
  • Technical depth: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small pretrained 594B parameters in just 68 hours on NVFP4, earning praise from Soumith Chintala

Sentiment blended celebration of funding and open-source wins with healthy skepticism toward benchmarks and pricing clarity. Policy voices like Nathan Lambert urged more careful AI discourse and Arthur Mensch urged European competitiveness.

entry.title: @TimDarcet @gabriberton The P in JEPA stands for predictive. The main distinction is not between JEA...
entry.summary: LeCun continues yesterday's Social thread, adding formal loss formulations and the history of anti-collapse methods. Yann LeCun (@ylecun) responds to a discussion by clarifying the taxonomy of joint-embedding architectures: the P in JEPA stands for predictive, and the fundamental distinction is not between JEA and JEPA but between joint-embedding approaches (predictive or not) and generative architectures. He lays out formal loss formulations: generative models predict y from x with a divergence loss between target and prediction, while JEA encodes both x and y and minimizes representation divergence with an anti-collapse regularizer R, useful when neither view has a privileged direction (e.g., two views of the same scene). He adds historical depth, citing Becker and Hinton's 1989 information-maximization anti-collapse model and noting Schmidhuber's early related work, and notes that whether a predictor is needed depends on the task.
